blocks.text: Grounding techniques go beyond a general instruction to use the provided context, covered in the previous topic, offering more specific, verifiable ways to tie a model claims directly to the actual retrieved evidence, requiring quotes, self-verification, and explicit extraction before generation.

This topic covers requiring direct quotes or exact spans from source material, having the model verify its own claims against the context, distinguishing directly stated facts from inferred ones, and structured extraction as a stronger grounding approach than instruction alone.
1. What Grounding Actually Means

blocks.alt: Building on retrieval prompting, grounding techniques tie claims to actual evidence

blocks.text: Grounding means every factual claim in a response can be traced back to something actually present in the retrieved source material, rather than the model general training knowledge or an unsupported inference presented as fact.
2. Grounded Claims vs Ungrounded Claims

blocks.alt: An ungrounded claim has no traceable source, a grounded claim traces to retrieved text

blocks.text: A grounded claim, "the return window is 30 days," directly reflects specific retrieved text, an ungrounded claim, stated with equal confidence, might come from the model general knowledge about typical return policies rather than the actual retrieved policy document, this distinction is exactly what grounding techniques aim to enforce.
3. Requiring Direct Quotes or Exact Spans

blocks.alt: Requiring a direct quote or an exact span from the source strengthens grounding

blocks.text: One of the strongest grounding techniques is explicitly requiring the model to quote the exact supporting text from the source alongside any factual claim, this makes ungrounded claims immediately visible, since a fabricated quote is far easier to spot as wrong than a fabricated paraphrase.

code.content:
prompt = (
    "For each claim in your answer, include the exact quoted sentence "
    "from the context that supports it. If no supporting quote exists, "
    "state that the context does not address this."
)

blocks.text: 4. Self-Verification Against the Context

blocks.alt: A model claim goes through a self verification step against context, becoming confirmed or retracted

blocks.text: This connects directly to the self-critique prompting technique covered in an earlier module, after generating an initial answer, asking the model to check each of its own claims specifically against the provided context, and retract or flag anything it cannot actually verify, adds a second grounding check beyond the initial generation.

blocks.text: 5. Distinguishing Directly Stated Facts From Inferences

blocks.alt: A directly stated fact in the source is distinguished from something inferred beyond what the source actually says

blocks.text: Not every reasonable sounding statement is actually directly supported, a source might state a product ships within 5 business days, an inference that it therefore always arrives before the weekend goes beyond what was actually stated, instructing the model to flag when it is inferring rather than directly quoting keeps this distinction visible.

blocks.title: This distinction matters more than it might first seem
blocks.content: A response that blends directly stated facts and reasonable sounding inferences without distinguishing them can mislead a reader into treating an inference with the same confidence as a directly supported fact.

blocks.text: 6. Grounding Through Structured Extraction Before Generation

blocks.alt: Relevant facts get extracted first, then generation happens only from those extracted facts

blocks.text: This connects directly to the prompt chaining technique covered in an earlier module, a stronger grounding approach splits the task into two chained steps, first extracting only the specific facts from the source that are relevant to the question, then generating the final answer using only those extracted facts as input, rather than the full original source text.
7. Grounding vs a Plain "Use the Context" Instruction

blocks.alt: A vague instruction to use the context is compared against a specific grounding requirement to quote and cite

blocks.text: This connects directly back to the retrieval prompting instruction covered in the previous topic, "answer using the provided context" is a reasonable starting instruction, but the specific grounding techniques covered in this topic, required quotes, self-verification, extraction first, provide meaningfully stronger, more verifiable guarantees than that general instruction alone.
8. Testing Whether a Response Is Actually Grounded

A practical test for grounding is checking whether every factual claim in a response can actually be located in the source material, if a quote requirement is in place, this check becomes mechanical, simply verifying the quoted text genuinely appears in the source, without a quote requirement, this check requires more careful manual review.
9. Grounding as a Foundation for Hallucination Reduction

These grounding techniques directly set up the next topic in this module, hallucination reduction, since a model reliably grounding its claims in traceable source evidence is one of the most direct and effective ways to reduce fabricated, unsupported claims in the first place.
Worked Example

A developer building a policy question answering tool finds occasional subtly wrong answers, the model sometimes states a plausible sounding but actually incorrect detail not present in the retrieved policy document.

Adding a requirement for the model to quote the exact supporting sentence for every factual claim makes these errors immediately visible, since a fabricated quote simply does not match anything in the actual source text, allowing the team to catch and further tighten the prompt against this specific failure pattern.
Common Mistakes

items: Relying only on a general "use the context" instruction instead of a stronger, verifiable grounding technique
Not distinguishing between a directly stated fact and a reasonable sounding inference in the response
Skipping a self-verification pass that could catch an ungrounded claim before it reaches a user
Assuming a response with confident sounding language is automatically grounded, without actually checking it against the source

blocks.text: Practice

Take a retrieval prompt you have built or could build, add a requirement for the model to quote the exact supporting text for each claim, and test it with a question that the provided context only partially addresses, checking whether the model correctly flags what it cannot verify.
Key Takeaway

Grounding techniques, requiring direct quotes, self-verification against context, distinguishing stated facts from inferences, and structured extraction before generation, provide meaningfully stronger, more verifiable guarantees that a response actually traces back to retrieved evidence than a general instruction to use the context alone.
